heuristics.rule: Get the level code, not just the title
heuristics.condition: When evaluating any PM offer across companies...
heuristics.action: ...ask for the numeric or alphanumeric level code (L5, IC5, ICT4) and cross-reference it against the company's internal leveling structure before comparing to your current role
heuristics.because: Titles like 'Senior PM' are internally defined and not portable — the same title can represent radically different scope and compensation across companies

heuristics.rule: Use compensation as a level verification signal
heuristics.condition: When a company states a title but the total comp offer seems off...
heuristics.action: ...check levels.fyi to verify the offer aligns with the median total comp for that stated level at that specific company
heuristics.because: If comp is below median for the stated level, the company may be soft-downleveling you while maintaining a flattering title

heuristics.rule: Ignore startup titles entirely; ask about decision rights instead
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a startup offer with an elevated title (Director, VP)...
heuristics.action: ...ask 'What decisions can I make unilaterally? Who has override authority over the roadmap?' and map the answer to an equivalent FAANG scope level
heuristics.because: Startups use inflated titles as compensation substitutes for cash; the title signals nothing reliable about actual scope or organizational influence

heuristics.rule: A promotion without scope increase is a title bump, not a career move
heuristics.condition: When receiving an internal promotion where the new level has the same scope as the current role...
heuristics.action: ...treat it as a lateral and evaluate whether it creates overleveling risk for future external moves
heuristics.because: An elevated title without expanded scope can make you look overleveled to future hiring managers who will ask about actual scope, not titles

heuristics.rule: Amazon L-numbers run one level inflated relative to FAANG peers
heuristics.condition: When comparing Amazon PM levels to Google or Meta...
heuristics.action: ...subtract one level from Amazon's code to find the scope equivalent (Amazon L6 ≈ Google L5 ≈ Meta IC5)
heuristics.because: Amazon's L-scale is inflated relative to peer companies, so direct number comparisons create false equivalencies

heuristics.rule: Validate a downlevel by requiring a defined upgrade path with a stated timeline
heuristics.condition: When considering accepting a lower title at a target company...
heuristics.action: ...only accept if the company provides explicit promotion criteria and a typical time-to-promo for moving to the next level
heuristics.because: Without a stated upgrade path, a downlevel at a prestigious company may become a permanent level reset rather than a temporary step

heuristics.rule: Test whether a lateral is actually a promotion by imagining the next hiring manager's reaction
heuristics.condition: When unsure whether a same-title move is a real step up...
heuristics.action: ...ask 'Would a hiring manager at my next target company look at this new title and comp and consider me a more qualified candidate?'
heuristics.because: Career moves only compound if each step makes the next step easier; a move that doesn't improve external perception isn't advancing the career trajectory

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Titles are cosmetic and company-specific; level codes map to actual scope, compensation bands, and promotion timelines that can be compared across companies
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask directly for the numeric or alphanumeric level code and cross-reference against a known leveling map (e.g., the FAANG equivalency table in this source)

decision_factors.factor: Total compensation vs. market median for that level
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Comp below the median for a stated level signals either a soft downlevel or a company underpaying relative to its own bands — both are red flags
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Look up levels.fyi median total comp for the specific company and level code; flag any offer more than 10–15% below median

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Real scope is defined by what decisions you can make unilaterally without escalation, not by what the title or org chart implies
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask: 'What decisions can I make without approval?' and 'Who has override authority over my roadmap or prioritization?'

decision_factors.why_it_matters: A lower title at a higher-tier company can open more future doors than a higher title at a lower-tier company, making the brand itself a compensating factor
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess whether hiring managers at your next target companies would respond more favorably to the new company's name on your resume

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Accepting a downlevel only makes sense if there is a clear, stated path and realistic timeline back to your target level
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask: 'What are the stated promotion criteria from this level to the next, and what is the typical time-to-promo for high performers?'

decision_factors.factor: Scope size relative to current role
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A lower title with materially larger scope is a real promotion; a higher title with smaller scope is a real demotion regardless of what the offer letter says
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Compare team size, product complexity, cross-functional reach, and autonomy between current and target roles

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Startup titles often come with equity as the intended compensation premium, but equity value is highly uncertain and should not be treated as equivalent to cash or vested RSUs
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Model equity at 0%, 1x, and 5x outcomes; only count equity as a compensating factor if the base + cash comp alone is acceptable

decision_factors.why_it_matters: An inflated title from a lower-tier company can make a PM look overleveled to hiring managers at target companies, reducing hiring appeal for roles that would actually be the right fit
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask whether future target company hiring managers would view the current title as appropriately scoped or suspiciously senior

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting an elevated startup title (VP, Director) for equity upside
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The inflated title can create overleveling problems when returning to large tech — hiring managers see a VP title from a 30-person company and either discount the scope or expect VP-level compensation that the candidate can't justify
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Mid-career PMs who plan to use startup experience as a stepping stone back into FAANG or large tech

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Taking an internal promotion that is a title bump without scope increase
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The elevated title makes the PM look overleveled for roles they could realistically land, while the lack of real scope growth means they haven't built the skills to justify the title externally
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs at companies with loose promotion criteria who plan to leverage the title in an external job search within 1–2 years

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a downlevel at a prestigious company without a stated upgrade path
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The downlevel may become permanent if promotion criteria are opaque or if the org changes; the PM resets their compensation trajectory and may spend 2–3 years recovering to their previous level
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs who accept FAANG downlevels expecting fast promotion but land in orgs with slow or competitive promotion processes

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Comparing offers using title alone without checking level codes
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: A PM may accept what appears to be a lateral or step up based on the title while actually taking a scope and compensation downgrade that takes years to reverse
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs earlier in their careers who haven't yet learned that titles are not standardized across company boundaries

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Moving from management back to IC at a new company
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Requires accepting a senior IC level while rebuilding a product work track record, which can feel like a step backward and delays return to management-track compensation and influence
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs who moved into management and want to return to IC work, especially those who found management less fulfilling than expected

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting a title without verifying the level code or compensation band
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: PMs anchor on familiar title language ('Senior PM') and assume cross-company equivalence, not realizing titles are internally defined
failure_patterns.consequence: The PM accepts what they believe is a lateral or promotion but has actually taken a scope and compensation downgrade that compounds negatively over time
warning_signs: Offer letter uses a title but no level code is provided or volunteered
Total comp is noticeably below levels.fyi median for the stated title at that company

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating a startup VP or Director title as equivalent to a FAANG staff or principal role
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Startups deliberately use senior titles as compensation substitutes, and PMs mistake the title for a signal of actual scope and influence
failure_patterns.consequence: When the PM tries to leverage the startup title for a FAANG return, hiring managers discount the scope, and the PM faces downleveling back to Senior PM despite years of elapsed time
warning_signs: The startup has fewer than 50 employees but is offering a VP or Director PM title
The role description has the CEO or founder listed as the ultimate product decision-maker

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting a downlevel without securing a defined promotion path
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates are so motivated by the brand or comp upside that they rationalize the downlevel as temporary without getting explicit commitments on timeline or criteria
failure_patterns.consequence: The PM spends 2–3 years at a lower level due to opaque promotion processes, competitive calibration, or org changes, effectively resetting their career trajectory
warning_signs: Recruiter or hiring manager gives vague answers about promotion timelines ('it depends on performance')
No written or formally stated promotion criteria exist for moving from the offered level to the next

failure_patterns.pattern: Benchmarking Amazon L5 as equivalent to Google L5 due to matching number
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: PMs assume level numbers are standardized across companies and do direct numeric comparisons without knowing that Amazon's scale is inflated
failure_patterns.consequence: A PM moving from Amazon L5 to Google L4 believes they have been downleveled when they have actually been leveled appropriately for their scope
warning_signs: PM compares offer levels by number alone without checking scope equivalency tables
PM expresses surprise or offense at a Google L4 offer after holding Amazon L5

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the level code for this role, and what is the next level code above it?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the company can articulate its own leveling structure clearly and whether the PM knows how to navigate it
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What are the stated promotion criteria and typical time-to-promo from this level to the next?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Treat this as a red flag — companies without clear level codes often have opaque promotion processes that favor incumbents over new hires

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the total compensation for this offer, and how does it compare to the levels.fyi median for this level at this company?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the company is offering within its own band or soft-downleveling by underpaying relative to the stated title
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Confirm the comp is at or above median; if significantly above, understand why (competing offer, specialized skills, or org urgency)
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Probe whether the lower comp reflects a lower actual level than the title suggests, or a company-wide compensation issue

diagnostic_questions.question: Who has final override authority over the roadmap and prioritization for this role?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: The real scope and autonomy of the role, which can differ dramatically from what the title implies
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If the answer is 'you do,' map this to a staff or principal equivalent scope regardless of title
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If the answer is 'the CEO' or 'a more senior PM,' the role has less scope than the title implies

diagnostic_questions.question: What level did the last person in this role hold, and why did they leave?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the company is trying to backfill with someone appropriately leveled or is attempting to hire above the role's actual scope
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If the previous person was at a lower level, ask why the company is now hiring higher
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If the company can't answer, it may indicate poor people-process discipline or that the role is newly created without clear scope definition

diagnostic_questions.question: Is this move increasing total compensation by more than 20%?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the financial upside is sufficient to justify any title or scope tradeoff
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: A 20%+ comp increase with brand upgrade is likely worth a title downlevel; evaluate scope and upgrade path
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If comp is flat or declining and the title is the same or lower, the move has no compensating factors and the decision rests entirely on scope and future optionality

industry_realities.common_belief: The same title at different companies represents the same level of seniority and scope
industry_realities.actual_reality: Titles are internally defined and not portable; 'Senior PM' at Google (L5) is roughly equivalent in scope to what many other companies call a mid-level PM, and 'Senior PM' at Amazon is L6, not L5
industry_realities.implication: Always translate titles into level codes and cross-reference against a known equivalency map before comparing offers or accepting a role

industry_realities.common_belief: A higher title is always a career step forward
industry_realities.actual_reality: A promotion in title without scope increase is a lateral at best; an inflated title from a lower-tier company can actively harm future hiring prospects by creating overleveling optics
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate career moves by scope, compensation, and future optionality — not by whether the title on the offer letter sounds more senior

industry_realities.common_belief: Startups offer senior titles because the roles are genuinely more senior
industry_realities.actual_reality: Startups inflate titles because they cannot compete on cash compensation; a 'VP of Product' at a 30-person startup may have less organizational reach than an L6 Staff PM at Meta
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate startup offers by decision rights and scope, not by title; model equity at conservative outcomes before treating it as real compensation

industry_realities.common_belief: Amazon L5 and Google L5 are equivalent because they share the same number
industry_realities.actual_reality: Amazon's L-scale runs inflated relative to FAANG peers; Amazon L5 is approximately equivalent to Google L4 and Meta IC4 in scope
industry_realities.implication: When moving between Amazon and other FAANG companies, expect and accept level code differences that look like downlevels but are actually accurate scope mappings

industry_realities.common_belief: Accepting a lower title at a new company is always a career step backward
industry_realities.actual_reality: A title downlevel at a higher-tier company can represent a real career step forward if total comp increases significantly, scope is materially larger, or brand opens future doors that the previous company could not
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate downlevel offers on the full package — comp trajectory, scope, brand, and defined upgrade path — not on the title comparison alone

industry_realities.common_belief: Total comp on the offer letter represents what you'll earn
industry_realities.actual_reality: If total comp is below the levels.fyi median for the stated level at that company, the offer may reflect a soft downlevel or below-band placement that signals how the company actually values the hire
industry_realities.implication: Always verify offer comp against levels.fyi medians for that specific company and level code; treat below-median comp as a diagnostic signal, not just a negotiation opportunity

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they evaluate an offer's level
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Reads the title on the offer letter and compares it to their current title to determine whether it's a step up, lateral, or down
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Asks for the level code, cross-references against a known equivalency map, verifies comp against levels.fyi median, and evaluates scope and decision rights independently of the title
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Junior evaluation leads to accepting apparent promotions that are actually laterals or downgrades; senior evaluation surfaces the real career impact of the move

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Is attracted to or concerned about the title (VP, Director) and models equity optimistically as a primary compensation factor
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Ignores the title entirely, asks specifically about decision rights and override authority, and models equity conservatively — accepting the role only if base and cash comp alone are satisfactory
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Overweighting titles and equity at startups can lock a PM into a role that looks impressive on paper but creates overleveling problems and doesn't deliver financial upside

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they think about accepting a downlevel
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Views any title downlevel as a step backward and declines on principle, or accepts without securing explicit promotion criteria and timeline
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Evaluates whether the downlevel is compensated by a tier jump, scope jump, or comp increase, and only accepts if a defined upgrade path with stated timeline is part of the offer
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Reflexive rejection of downlevels causes PMs to miss real career advances; accepting without an upgrade path turns a temporary step into a permanent reset

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they interpret cross-company level numbers
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Compares level numbers directly across companies (Amazon L5 = Google L5) and feels downleveled or overleveled when the numbers differ
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Knows the equivalency offsets (Amazon runs one level inflated; Google L5 ≈ Amazon L6) and translates level codes into scope terms before making any comparison
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Direct number comparisons lead to misreading offers, unnecessary negotiation friction, and potentially declining appropriately-leveled roles at target companies

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they determine the 'real' level of a role
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Relies on the title and job description to infer scope and seniority
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Asks the four diagnostic questions: level code, promotion criteria and time-to-promo, levels of PMs they'd work with, and the level of the previous person in the role
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Job descriptions are marketing; the four diagnostic questions surface the structural reality of the role, including whether the company is trying to underhire or overhire for the position
